desc:
The string street describes a row of plots. A plot is either a house H or an empty plot .. You may put a water bucket on any empty plot (at most one per plot).

A house is served if there is a bucket on the plot immediately to its left or immediately to its right. Return the minimum number of buckets needed so that every house is served, or -1 if that cannot be done.

"H..H"    -> 2
".H.H."   -> 1
".HHH."   -> -1

In the second example a single bucket on the middle plot serves both houses.
hints: When is the answer -1? Look at a house whose both neighbours are houses or walls.
Process houses from left to right. For the leftmost unserved house, a bucket on its right neighbour is at least as good as one on its left neighbour. Why?
For an unserved house at i: if i+1 is empty, put a bucket there (it also serves a house at i+2, so jump to i+3); else if i-1 is empty, put a bucket there; otherwise return -1.
editorial: Sweep from left to right. Whenever you meet a house that is not yet served, you must place a bucket next to it. Everything to its left is already served, so a bucket on the left neighbour can only help this one house. A bucket on the right neighbour also helps the house at i + 2 if there is one. Hence the right neighbour is never worse (exchange argument), and we use the left one only when the right one is blocked.

Implementation: at a house at index i, if i + 1 exists and is ., add a bucket and move to i + 3 (the plot i + 2, if a house, is served). Otherwise if i > 0 and i - 1 is ., add a bucket and move to i + 1; if neither neighbour is empty return -1. A left-neighbour bucket is never placed on a plot that already holds one, because a bucket placed to the right of the earlier house makes us skip the next house. O(n) time, O(1) space.
